record.title: A preprint reports gains from adapting agent skills to executor capability
record.summary: A 24-page arXiv preprint reports that reusable agent skills can help stronger models while providing little benefit or even reducing scores for weaker executors. Across 607 tasks in SkillsBench, DocOps and Tessl, the authors selected 103 skill-sensitive task-skill pairs and mapped failures to tool execution, context management, instruction following and verification. A fixed meta-skill used to adapt skill wording improved three weak executors in one-shot tests when applied by stronger rewriters; in a five-round self-evolution experiment, the meta-skill arm finished above the no-meta arm for all seven executors. These are author-reported benchmark results, not independently reproduced outcomes; each model-task-condition cell was run once in the described experiments. The authors’ project page now links a public reproduction repository with task indexes and experiment code, but this activation did not pin or run it.
organizations: University of Chinese Academy of Sciences

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: arXiv hosts a 24-page v1 preprint submitted on 2026-10-10 that studies capability-dependent effects of agent skills and skill adaptation.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Across 607 tasks from SkillsBench, DocOps and Tessl, the authors select 103 skill-sensitive task-skill pairs and report that injected skills can substantially help stronger models while leaving weaker models nearly unchanged or harming them; 86% of failed weak-model runs on the selected pairs violate requirements already stated in the skill.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In one-shot adaptation on the 103 selected pairs, the authors report that capable rewriters using their meta-skill improve the mean scores of three weaker executors; Kimi-K3 raises Gemma-4-E4B from 0.029 to 0.170, while the weak executors’ own rewrites score below the original-skill baseline on average.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: In a five-round self-evolution experiment, the meta-skill arm ends above the no-meta arm for all seven tested executors, with reported round-five differences of 0.020–0.051 in average task score.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The preprint does not establish repeat-run stability, independent reproduction, transfer to untested executors or benchmarks, benefits when skills must be retrieved, or effects from updating model parameters.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: The author project page links a public MIT-licensed reproduction repository containing benchmark task indexes, configuration and instructions for evaluation, skill adaptation and self-evolution. This activation inspected the repository page and README but did not execute its code.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent reproduction or repeated-run variance estimate was inspected; the paper reports each model-task-condition cell once.

A public author reproduction repository is now available, with task indexes, source revision/checksum metadata and experiment commands. This activation did not pin a commit, audit code paths or run the repository; source-only tests would not reproduce model outcomes.
Skill retrieval and progressive disclosure are out of scope; tasks use skills already supplied in context, and multiple skills are sometimes evaluated as a bundle.

brief.importance_rationale: If the reported results hold, adapting instructions and revision guidance to executor capability could improve agent task outcomes across heterogeneous models, affecting skill and harness design. The consequence is meaningful for agent engineering, but the evidence is one preprint with single-run cells and no independent reproduction.
limitations: The preprint’s benchmark results are author-reported and have not been independently reproduced here.
The 103 task-skill pairs are selected as skill-sensitive from an initial 607-task set; results on this selected subset do not represent all tasks.
Each model-task-condition cell is run once. The authors say exact effect sizes of the five-round comparison should not be overinterpreted.
The study evaluates skills already supplied to the executor; retrieval and progressive disclosure are outside scope. Some comparisons treat bundles of multiple skills as one pair.

A public author reproduction repository is now linked from the project page. This activation did not pin its commit, audit its code, run its tests or reproduce model outcomes; provider endpoints and benchmark environments can affect results.

brief.summary: A 24-page arXiv preprint reports that reusable agent skills can help stronger models while providing little benefit or even reducing scores for weaker executors. Across 607 tasks in SkillsBench, DocOps and Tessl, the authors selected 103 skill-sensitive task-skill pairs and mapped failures to tool execution, context management, instruction following and verification. A fixed meta-skill used to adapt skill wording improved three weak executors in one-shot tests when applied by stronger rewriters; in a five-round self-evolution experiment, the meta-skill arm finished above the no-meta arm for all seven executors. These are author-reported benchmark results, not independently reproduced outcomes; each model-task-condition cell was run once in the described experiments. The authors’ project page now links a public reproduction repository with task indexes and experiment code, but this activation did not pin or run it.

technical.claimed_result: The authors report capability-dependent effects of injected skills across seven models and three benchmarks, positive one-shot adaptation results for weaker executors under capable rewriters, and positive final-round score gaps for all seven executors in a five-round self-evolution comparison using their meta-skill.
technical.demonstrated_result: The publication and its described protocol, tables and scope are directly inspectable in the arXiv v1 preprint. The experimental performance outcomes remain paper-reported claims, not independently demonstrated results in this record.
technical.implementation_status: Research preprint v1 submitted to arXiv on 2026-10-10. The author project page now links a public MIT-licensed GitHub repository containing reproduction code, task indexes and experiment commands. This activation inspected the repository landing page and README but did not pin a commit, audit code paths or execute tests/experiments.
technical.mechanism: The paper diagnoses weak-executor failures as tool execution, context management, instruction-following and verification problems. A fixed task-independent meta-skill directs a capable rewriter or a self-evolution loop to revise skill wording around those failure modes; the underlying model parameters are not updated.
technical.novelty: The study examines strong-to-weak model mismatch in skill use and applies a fixed failure-mode-guided rewrite protocol to both one-shot skill adaptation and iterative self-evolution. It reports positive round-five differences for all seven tested executors but does not establish broad transfer.
technical.regime: 607 tasks from SkillsBench, DocOps and Tessl; 103 selected skill-sensitive task-skill pairs; seven executor models. One-shot rewriting tests three weaker executors and four capable rewriters. Self-evolution tests seven executors for five rounds. Tasks use skills already in context; benchmark-native verifiers or an LLM judge score outcomes.
technical.reproducibility: The preprint describes methods, rewrite protocol, validity checks, full meta-skill and baseline prompts. A public author repository now provides task indexes, source revision/checksum metadata, model configuration and evaluation/adaptation/evolution commands, including repeated-run options. The repository was not executed or independently audited here; outcome reproduction remains open.
technical.strongest_baseline: For one-shot adaptation, original unrevised skills and a one-sentence rewriting prompt are comparison arms. For self-evolution, the authors compare the meta-skill loop with the same executor revising without the meta-skill and with a same-window baseline rerunning the original skill.

brief.title: A preprint reports gains from adapting agent skills to executor capability
brief.why_it_matters: The paper makes a useful distinction between having relevant procedural guidance and an executor being able to act on it. If replicated, capability-matched skill wording and trajectory-based revision could change how agent harnesses are designed and evaluated. The study covers supplied skills and selected task pairs; it does not test skill retrieval or progressive disclosure, and its self-evolution runs are single rollout per cell.
